name: Bianca Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Right now I'm foreman on a transmission crew, so the big steel towers, not the poles along the street. This month we're restringing a 132,000-volt line across the hills north of the city, which means a week in a roadside hotel, up at five, harnesses checked, and then six of us climbing sixty metres with the wind trying to peel you off. I love the view and I love that my crew trusts me. What wears me out is the hotel food and missing home four nights a week.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how does the money side look?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sam, my partner, teaches maths at a secondary school across town. We rent a two-bed in Eastfield with a balcony full of her tomato plants. We've got about three months of savings, which sounds fine until you remember the van needed a new gearbox last year. I'm also the health and safety rep for our branch of the union, which takes up more evenings than Sam would like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the robots stay in the films. Fair enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I say now: AI is good for writing up a near-miss report at the end of a long day and not much else. At union meetings I'd say let's stop worrying about chatbots and start worrying about crew sizes and hotel allowances. Online I'd probably just post a photo from the top of a tower and leave it at that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be relieved. Our work is about steel, wind and people who trust each other, and that stays the same. The pressures I already have don't go away, like the travel and the fact that the company keeps trying to squeeze a six-person job into five. But money-wise we're steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing the job and keep the union work going. I'd keep using the AI thing for my incident reports, because it does save me an hour on a Friday. Sam and I would keep putting about three hundred a month aside, and in a couple of years we'd talk about kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little bored by the whole AI topic, honestly, the way you get bored of a weather warning that never comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the company squeezes six-person jobs into five. What happens then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The fifth person does the work of the sixth, and they get tired, and tired climbers drop things. Last year a spanner fell forty metres and landed a metre from my apprentice, and that came from a staffing spreadsheet, not a robot. That's the fight I'd still be having.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned kids. Does this picture change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it keeps it on track. Sam wants to be a mum by thirty-two, and in this world I can see us doing it. I'd want to come off the travelling crew by then, maybe onto local maintenance.

say: I'd say AI is handy for **incident reports** and not much else.
I'd tell the union to focus on **crew sizes** and hotel allowances instead.
think: I'd feel **relieved** because tower work stays about steel, wind and trust.
My existing pressures, **travel and short crews**, would still be there.
do: Keep using AI to save about **an hour** on Friday reports.
Keep saving about **three hundred a month** with Sam.
Plan to talk about **having kids** in a couple of years.
feel: **Calm**, and a bit bored of AI talk, like a warning that never comes.
S0.quote: Last year a spanner fell forty metres and landed a metre from my apprentice, and that came from a staffing spreadsheet, not a robot.
fieldNote: She already uses AI **now and then** for paperwork, without fuss.
Her stories are about **safety and staffing**, which she sees as the real risks.
A stable **household plan** with Sam sits behind her calm.

steps.text: Keep running the transmission crew and union safety work
Put about three hundred a month into joint savings with Sam
Plan to move to local maintenance before starting a family

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Planning and checking. That's the office and the engineers, but it's also some of my day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At work I'd say the union needs to be in the room when they bring in the planning software, not after. To friends I'd say line work is fine but it'll look different, more tablets, more drones. Online I'd share stories about teachers too, because that's Sam's world and I think she'd feel it before me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, the drones already do half our inspections, and the outage planning is clearly next for software. I'd be fine on the steel for years. What I'd worry about is Sam: a lot of teaching is writing, checking and planning, exactly what's on that list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sign up for the company's drone inspection course in the first few months, since it's free and I'd rather fly the thing than be replaced by it. I'd use AI more for my crew briefings and switching paperwork once a couple of other foremen had tried it. And I'd push for a branch agreement on how the new software rolls out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Mostly for Sam, a bit for me. Like seeing a crack in a tower foot that's probably fine but you note it anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Sam say if you told her you were worried for her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say the kids still need a person in the room, and she's right. But schools love saving money as much as power companies do. My partner Sam marks two hundred maths books a week, and that is exactly the kind of checking AI gets told to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, our planner who travels with us. He does the permits, the landowner calls and the outage bookings, and that's the whole list on your card. He's fifty-one and he's never done anything else.

say: I'd tell the union to be **in the room** before planning software arrives.
I'd tell friends line work stays, with **more drones** and tablets.
think: Drones already do **half our inspections**, and outage planning is next.
My bigger worry is **Sam's teaching**, which is full of checking and planning.
do: Take the free **drone inspection course** in the first few months.
Use AI for **crew briefings** once other foremen have tested it.
Push for a **branch agreement** on how planning software rolls out.
feel: **Uneasy**, mostly for Sam, like a small crack you note anyway.
S1.quote: My partner Sam marks two hundred maths books a week, and that is exactly the kind of checking AI gets told to do.
fieldNote: She waits for **proof from peers** before using AI more, fitting her steady style.
Her worry shifts to the **household**, since teaching is high on thinking tasks.
She names **Dev the planner** as the colleague most at risk.

steps.text: Sign up for the company's free drone inspection course
Use AI for crew briefings after other foremen try it
Push the union branch for a software rollout agreement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2028 for the AI, 2031 for robots. Sam goes first and then me. That's the house, both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it at every union meeting: we need a shared plan for workers, not just a plan for shareholders. With the crew I'd keep the safety rules tight, because scared people cut corners. Online I'd probably be one of those people posting about a basic income, which I never thought I'd be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The thinking side of my job, the planning, the permits, the reports, goes in 2028, and I'd keep the climbing until about 2031. But Sam's job is mostly thinking work, so our household loses an income straight away. We'd go from two steady wages to one wage with a three-year clock on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the baby plans for now, which would break Sam's heart. We'd move every spare penny into savings and cut the second car, since the van can do both. I'd push hard for the union and Sam's teachers' union to work together on a transition fund, and I'd ask the company whether they need people to supervise and fix the tower robots when they come.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing sums, and I'm not someone who lies awake. The worst bit is that I can't fix Sam's part with my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd ask about supervising the robots. Do you think that job would exist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while, yes, someone has to sign off a line before it goes live. But one supervisor for ten machines, not one for each. I'd be fighting six good climbers for that one seat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holiday to Sam's family in the summer, then the second car, then the gym. We wouldn't touch the rent, because moving would cost more than staying. And I'd stop eating at the hotel restaurant and bring sandwiches, which sounds small but it's forty a week.

say: I'd tell union meetings we need a **plan for workers**, not just shareholders.
I'd probably start posting about **basic income**, which surprises me.
think: My **planning and permits** go in 2028 and climbing lasts until about 2031.
Sam's teaching is mostly thinking work, so we **lose an income** first.
do: Pause the **baby plans** and move every spare penny into savings.
Sell the **second car** and cut the summer holiday.
Ask the company about **supervising tower robots** when they arrive.
feel: **Alarmed** and sleepless, because she can't fix Sam's side with her hands.
S2.quote: We'd go from two steady wages to one wage with a three-year clock on it.
fieldNote: Her fear centres on the **household**, not only her own climbing.
The **thinking-first** timing means her partner loses work before she does.
She shifts politically toward **basic income** and cross-union action.
She sees robot supervision as real but with **few seats**.

steps.text: Put the plan to have a baby on hold
Sell the second car and skip the summer holiday
Work with Sam's teachers' union on a joint transition fund
Apply to supervise tower robots before they arrive

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Sam's job goes in 2031, mine around 2034. That at least gives us a bit of room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the window, so let's use it, both unions together. To friends I'd say I'm learning the robot side now, while I still have a job to learn it in. Online, the same as always, but less angry than in the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means Sam can keep teaching while she looks around, and I've got eight years of steel. I think we'd still have the baby, just maybe in 2028 instead of later, so the kid is in school before everything shifts. It sounds mad to plan a baby around robots, but that's what I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the drone course this year and then push to get onto the company's pilot team for tower-climbing robots, if they run one. We'd lift savings from three months to six by 2029. Sam would start a part-time course in school counselling, which seems more about people than checking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a way I can work with. With five years warning I can plan a baby, a course and a savings target, and with two years I'd just be panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Sam would retrain. Is that her idea or yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mine, honestly, and I'd need to be careful how I raise it. She loves teaching maths. I'd bring it up over a Sunday breakfast and then shut up and let her think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it went badly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Governments that sat on their hands for five years. The companies are going to do what makes money, that's what they are. It's the job of politicians to make sure the money goes back to people somehow.

say: I'd say five years is **the window**, and both unions should use it together.
I'd tell friends I'm learning **the robot side** while I still can.
think: Five years gives Sam time and me **eight years of steel**.
We'd likely have **the baby in 2028**, before everything shifts.
do: Finish the **drone course** this year and join any tower-robot pilot team.
Lift savings from **three to six months** by 2029.
Encourage Sam to study **school counselling** part time.
feel: **Anxious** but workable, because time allows a real plan.
S3.quote: With five years warning I can plan a baby, a course and a savings target, and with two years I'd just be panicking.
fieldNote: Warning time turns her panic into a **sequenced plan**: baby, course, savings.
She knowingly takes the **lead on Sam's career**, and admits it.
She blames **slow governments** more than companies.

steps.text: Join the company's pilot team for tower-climbing robots
Build savings from three to six months by 2029
Try for a baby in 2028 before the change lands
Finish the drone inspection course this year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: 2036 and robots in 2039. I'd be thirty-nine. That's a different conversation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a decade, so let's get the training funds and the transition rules written now. At the depot I'd be the one telling the young ones to get a second skill. Online I'd mostly post about the grid needing more people this decade, which it does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough for me to do the travelling job, come off it, and move into something like robot fleet supervision or grid planning. Sam would have ten years of teaching and time to retrain if she wanted. Honestly, I'd sleep fine most nights.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the drone course, then in a few years a part-time engineering certificate, the kind the company pays half of. We'd have the baby as planned and buy a small flat around 2029. I'd keep my union role so I'm in the room when the robot rules get written.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, quietly. It's more like a long-range forecast than a storm warning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything you'd do differently even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop telling the apprentices this is a job for life. I tell every new apprentice that tower climbing will feed you for a decade, so use that decade to learn what comes after the climbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And would Sam stay in teaching?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if the kids still need someone in the room. She'd use the AI for the marking and keep the bit she loves. That's the version where we both come out fine.

say: I'd say we have **a decade** to write training funds and transition rules.
I'd tell young linemen to get **a second skill**.
think: Ten years lets me move to **robot fleet supervision** or grid planning.
Sam gets **ten years of teaching** and time to retrain.
do: Take a **part-time engineering certificate** the company half pays for.
Have the baby as planned and **buy a small flat** around 2029.
Keep the **union role** to help write the robot rules.
feel: Quietly **uneasy**, like a long-range forecast rather than a warning.
S4.quote: I tell every new apprentice that tower climbing will feed you for a decade, so use that decade to learn what comes after the climbing.
fieldNote: With ten years she sees a **clean handover** from climbing to supervision.
She drops the **job for life** message to apprentices, a real shift for her.
Her household plans go ahead, so her **mood eases** a lot.

steps.text: Start a part-time engineering certificate with company funding
Buy a small flat with Sam around 2029
Stay union safety rep to shape the robot rules

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without any doubt, because it hits Sam first and me three years later, so there's no year when we're both safe. What would help is the two unions working together on a transition fund, and a real promise that people like me get first go at the robot supervision jobs. I can climb a sixty-metre tower in a gale, but I can't stop a school deciding a computer marks the books.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the travelling. Half of why I'd jump at a supervisor job is to sleep in my own bed. If robots took the hotel weeks and left me the interesting bit, I'd honestly be happy.

headlineQuote: I can climb a sixty-metre tower in a gale, but I can't stop a school deciding a computer marks the books.
portrait: Bianca is a **27-year-old transmission foreman** who climbs sixty-metre towers and is her union branch's safety rep.
She lives with **Sam, a maths teacher**, and they plan a baby within a few years.
She uses AI **now and then** for reports and adopts new tools once other foremen have tested them.
Her biggest fear is the **household**, because Sam's thinking work goes before her own climbing.
With more warning she plans a **steady move** toward drones, robot supervision and engineering study.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because Sam's teaching goes first and her own climbing follows three years later.
whatWouldHelp: A **joint union transition fund** and first chance at robot supervision jobs for experienced climbers.
